Nickel-Catalyzed Enantioconvergent Allenylic Amination of Allenols
Activated by Hydrogen-Bonding Interaction with Methanol
Wen-Qian Zhang
+
, Zihan Lin
+
, Danxing Wu, Yuhao Wang, Hajime Hirao, and
Liu-Zhu Gong*
Abstract: The ubiquitous nature of amines in drug
compounds, bioactive molecules and natural products
has fueled intense interest in their synthesis. Herein, we
introduce a nickel-catalyzed enantioconvergent allenylic
amination of methanol-activated allenols. This protocol
affords a diverse array of functionalized allenylic amines
in high yields and with excellent enantioselectivities.
The synthetic potential of this method is demonstrated
by employing bioactive amines as nucleophiles and
conducting gram-scale reactions. Furthermore, mecha-
nistic investigations and DFT calculations elucidate the
role of methanol as an activator in the nickel-catalyzed
reaction, facilitating the oxidative addition of the C � O
bond of allenols through hydrogen-bonding interactions.
The remarkable outcomes arise from a rapid racemiza-
tion of allenols enabled by the nickel catalyst and from
highly enantioselective dynamic kinetic asymmetric
transformation of η
3
-alkadienylnickel intermediates.
Introduction
The amines are a critical component of a wide range of
existing drug compounds, bioactive molecules, and anti-
cancer agents, contributing significantly to their diverse
biological and pharmacological activities. Remarkably, more
than 80 % of U.S. FDA-approved pharmaceuticals contain
amine fragments.
[1]
Typical methods for incorporating an
amine moiety into carbon chains include nucleophilic
substitution reactions of amines with alkyl halides (or
pseudohalides), reductive amination, and transition-metal-
catalyzed C � N cross coupling reactions. Among these
methods, transition-metal-catalyzed allylic amination has
emerged as a widely utilized technique for the precise
construction of C(sp
3
) � N bonds with control over both
regio- and stereochemistry. However, the relatively strong
Lewis basicity of aliphatic amines leads to strong coordina-
tion with transition-metal catalysts in some cases, resulting
in catalyst poisoning and the suppression of key elementary
steps in the catalytic cycle. As such, enantioselective variants
of allylic amination reactions employing aliphatic amines,
enabled by transition-metal catalysis, have faced significant
limitations in their development and success.
[2]
On a related
note, while allenylic substitution reactions are conceptually
similar to transition-metal-catalyzed allylic substitution, they
are often more challenging to execute due to the formation
of less reactive η
3
-alkadienylmetal intermediates during the
oxidative addition of metal catalysts to allenylic substrates.
Palladium
[3]
and iridium
[4]
complexes are the most commonly
used catalysts. Upon reacting with racemic allenylic sub-
strates, a pair of diastereomeric η
3
-alkadienyl-palladium
complexes is formed. The two diastereomeric complexes can
rapidly interconvert to each other through a η
1
-alkadienyl-
metal complex intermediate, allowing a subsequent attack
by a nucleophile to give an enantioconvergent allenylic
product.
[3a–c,e,g–k,n]
In contrast, in a similar catalytic process
mediated by an iridium catalyst, the diastereomeric η
3
-
alkadienyliridium intermediates are captured by the nucleo-
philes prior to interconversion, thus leading to allenylation
products with retention of configuration and a kinetic
resolution of racemic allenylic reactants.
[4]
In addition, either
palladium
[5]
or iridium
[6]
complexes could also enable α-
branched racemic allenylic substrates to undergo stereo-
convergent allenylic substitution reactions (Scheme 1a).
Based on these general principles, a variety of enantioselec-
tive allenylic substitution reactions with a broad range of
soft nucleophiles have been developed.
[3b–e,g–k,m–p,5–6]
How-
ever, there is only a limited number of reports on
asymmetric allenylic amination between allenylic phos-
phates or carbonates and amines or amides enabled by
chiral palladium complex catalysis.
[3c,d,g,h,5b,6c]
On another
note, nickel, which features higher natural abundance,
chemical sustainability, and affordability compared to noble
metals, has emerged as an important alternative in catalysis
over last several decades.
[7]
Notably, nickel complexes allow
allylic alcohols to directly participate in asymmetric allylic
alkylation reactions without the need for external activators
of hydroxy groups (Scheme 1b).
[8]
This feature confers both
step- and atom-economy benefits. Surprisingly, nickel-cata-
lyzed allenylic substitution reactions to access axial products
have not yet been reported,
[9]
despite the well-established

In this study, we present the first nickel-catalyzed
enantioconvergent allenylic amination of allenols with a
broad substrate scope, accommodating a diverse range of
allenols and amines. The reaction is compatible with a
multitude of functional groups, drug fragments, and natural
products, yielding an extensive collection of allenylic amines
characterized by near-perfect yields and enantioselectivities
(Scheme 1c). Furthermore, mechanistic studies and density
functional theory (DFT) calculations indicate that a rapid
interchange between diastereomeric η
3
-alkadienylnickel in-
termediates allows an efficient dynamic kinetic asymmetric
transformation (DyKAT) that turns out to be the origin of
high enantioselectivity. In addition, the calculations suggest
that the activation of allenols is promoted by a hydrogen-
bonding interaction with methanol molecule, aiding the
oxidative addition of the nickel catalyst. Subsequently, the
resulting η
3
-alkadienylnickel intermediate undergoes amina-
tion through an outer-sphere amine-attack pathway.
Results and Discussion
Our initial research efforts were concentrated on optimizing
the nickel-catalyzed asymmetric allenylic amination between
a racemic allenol 1 and N-methylbenzyl amine 2. A system-
atic examination of the reaction parameters and ligands
identified a chiral nickel complex in situ formed from
Ni(cod)
2
and (S,S)-BenzP* to be the optimal catalyst (see
Tables S1–S4 in the Supporting Information for more de-
tails). In the presence of 3 mol % Ni(cod)
2
and 4 mol %
(S,S)-BenzP* and in a solvent mixture of chlorobenzene and
methanol, the reaction proceeded smoothly to afford the
desired allenylation product 3 in > 95 % NMR yield and
with 99 % ee (entry 1, Table 1). As anticipated, no reaction
was detected in the absence of the nickel catalyst (entry 2).
Interestingly, the reaction got much slower in the absence of
methanol, indicating that methanol is probably an external
activator for the hydroxyl group through a hydrogen-
bonding interaction (entry 3).
[11]
However, the presence of
chiral phosphoric acid was unable to speed up the reaction
while obvious difference in the stereochemical control was
found between (S) and (R)-TRIP
[12]
in chlorobenzene at
15 ° C (entries 4 and 5). The choice of nickel precursor also
had a profound impact on the reaction. Neither air-stable
nickel(0) nor nickel(II) pre-catalysts catalyzed this reaction
(entry 6). A minor modification in the ratio of 1 to 2
adversely affected the yield (entry 7). Adjusting either the
solvent or the nickel-to-ligand ratio failed to enhance the
reaction performance (entries 8 and 9).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, our
initial assessment aimed to explore the versatility of various
amines in conjunction with racemic 4-phenylbuta-2,3-dien-1-

showcased their capacity to participate in this protocol,
furnishing the corresponding (S)-allenylic amines in moder-
ate to good yields, with the ee values mostly exceeding 97 %.
Linear secondary amines (3–7) were well-tolerated, while
increased steric hindrance of amines resulting in significantly
reduced yields. Cyclic aliphatic amines of varying ring sizes,
encompassing azetidine, pyrrolidine, piperidine, 4-phenyl-
piperidine, azepane, and azocane (8–13), proved to be
efficient nucleophiles, with particularly noteworthy ee values
for piperidine or azocane (98 %). Furthermore, a spectrum
of six-membered heterocyclic amines (14–22) smoothly
underwent transformation, consistently yielding products
with > 97 % ee. Among these heterocyclic amines, both
morpholine and N-substituted piperazine are frequently
encountered in drug molecules.
[1b]
Cyclic aromatic amines,
such as indoline, also exhibited sufficient nucleophilicity to
engage in the allenylic amination reaction (23). However,
broadening the scope of the reaction to primary amines,
such as benzylamine, resulted in a significantly poorer
outcome, giving 24 with mere 15 % yield and 66 % ee.
Nevertheless, after another systematic optimization of
reaction conditions (see Tables S5 and S6 in the Supporting
Information for more details), 24 could be furnished with
synthetically valuable 54 % yield and 94 % ee. However,
anilines showed very poor reactivity, leading to trace
amounts of product presumably due to the low nucleophi-
licity (see Supporting Information).
We then shifted our focus toward exploring the range of
racemic allenols through the reaction with 1-phenylpiper-
azine 27. Various substituted phenyl groups bearing either
electron-donating or electron-withdrawing substituents (28–
35) were found to be compatible. In general, very high
enantioselectivity was achieved in all cases (95 to > 99 %
ee), although the yield appeared to correlate with the
electron density and steric hindrance of the phenyl group.
Consequently, the reaction with 35, bearing a para-cyano-
phenyl, provided a considerably lower yield. Importantly,
the reactions involving allenols substituted with alkyl groups
bearing primary, secondary, tertiary carbon (36–39) and
cyclic secondary carbon 40 all underwent the reaction
smoothly. Although only a moderate yield was obtained for
tBu-substituted allenol, it features the highest enantioselec-
tivity (> 99 % ee). More importantly, allenols carrying alkyl
groups with synthetically valuable functional groups, such as
internal alkene or terminal alkene (41 and 42), benzyl or
silyl ethers (43 and 44) and amides (45 and 46), proved to be
suitable reactants, furnishing multiply functionalized alle-
nylic amines with excellent enantioselectivities (94–97 % ee).
The absolute configuration of 34 was unambiguously
determined through X-ray crystallographic analysis.
[13]
We next assessed the applicability of this allenylic
amination process to the late-stage functionalization of
structurally complex molecules (Scheme 3). A dozen of
drugs, drug fragments, and natural products (48–59), featur-
ing diverse motifs, were successfully modified into their
corresponding allenylic amines in good yields and with
excellent stereoselectivities.
[14]
Notably, this protocol pro-
vides an efficient route to the optically pure allenylic analog
of naftifine 48. Particularly remarkable was the nearly
quantitative transformation of much more stable amine
hydrochlorides (53–56) into allenylic amines with excellent
enantioselectivity in the presence of Cs
2
CO
3
. To further
demonstrate the synthetic applicability, we tested gram-scale
reactions employing only 2 mol % of the chiral nickel
catalyst, which afforded the desired allenylic amines, main-
taining the yield and enantioselectivity almost at par with
the small-scale reaction.
To gain insight into the role of methanol in the
activation of allenol, a series of control experiments were
conducted. As shown in Scheme 4a, the addition of meth-
anol obviously accelerated the reaction (entries 1–3).
[15]

facilitate reactions involving ionic intermediates,

more specific interactions. Thus, a model reaction between 1
and 2 was conducted in a solvent mixture of chlorobenzene
and dichloromethane (1.52 : 1 volume ratio), which should

Moreover, kinetic order of each of reaction components,
including catalyst, was measured by means of differential
rate laws (Scheme 4c). A zero-order reaction was identified

Interestingly, the reaction order for methanol is 0.68,

C onclusion
In summary, we have developed a nickel-catalyzed enantio-
convergent allenylic amination of allenols, offering an
efficient route to a wide array of densely functionalized
allenylic amines in high yields and with excellent enantiose-
lectivities. Notably, this method allows for the incorporation
of bioactive amine fragment derivatives. Through mechanis-
tic studies and DFT calculations, we have unveiled the
pivotal role of methanol in activating the hydroxyl group,
leading to a rapid DyKAT process during the formation of
η
3
-alkadienylnickel intermediates. This enables the stereo-
convergent conversion of racemic allenols. The cooperative
activation of Ni/hydrogen-bonding interaction represents a
promising strategy for allenylic substitution reactions involv-
ing other nucleophiles beyond amines. The future explora-
tion of this field holds great promise.
